lessons.title: 1A. Print messages to the screen
lessons.subtitle: Learn one small thing at a time: showing output
lessons.focus: print(), strings in quotes, running top-to-bottom
lessons.concept: Programs are instructions that run from top to bottom. print() shows text on the screen. Text in Python is called a string (text) and must go inside quotes.
learning: Code runs in order from top to bottom
lessons.starter: print("Hello, world!")

tasks.prompt: Change the message to say Hello, Year 9!.

primm.predict: What will appear on the screen?
primm.investigate: print() sends the string inside the brackets to the output. The quotes mark the start and end of text.
primm.modify: Change the words inside the quotes.
primm.make: Make it print a greeting with your name.

lessons.title: 1B. Text must be in quotes
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: fix and use strings
lessons.concept: A string is a sequence of characters (text). In Python you can use single or double quotes. If your text contains an apostrophe, double quotes can make it easier.
learning: Strings (text) are data made of characters
Quotes tell Python where the text (string) starts and ends
lessons.starter:
print("Python is fun")
print('I am learning')

tasks.prompt: Add a print line that says It's a sunny day using double quotes.

lessons.title: 1C. Run in order
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: predict the order
lessons.concept: Python executes one line at a time from top to bottom. The order of your print statements controls the order of output.
learning: Each line runs after the previous one
lessons.starter:
print("First")
print("Second")
print("Third")

tasks.prompt: Reorder the lines so the output is Third, Second, First.
tasks.hint: Move the print lines into that order.

lessons.title: Section 1 Test: First program
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: print and sequencing
lessons.concept: Create a short program from scratch using print() and strings. This tests the core ideas from Section 1.
learning: Run lines in the correct order
lessons.starter:
# Section 1 Test
# Write your code below

tasks.prompt: Print exactly three lines in this order: Welcome, Python basics, Let's code!
tasks.hint: Use three print() statements, one per line.

lessons.title: 2A. Store values in variables
lessons.subtitle: Learn one small thing at a time: labels for values
lessons.concept: A variable stores a value in memory and gives it a name (label). You create/update it with =. You can change a variable's value later.
learning: age = 20 stores a value in a variable
lessons.starter:
age = 20
print(age)
age = 30
print(age)

tasks.prompt: Create a variable called score set to 10, print it, change it to 15, print it again.

lessons.title: 2B. Whole numbers: int
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: use whole numbers
lessons.concept: Integers (int) are whole numbers (no decimal point) like 0, 7, 20, -3. You can store them in variables and print them.
learning: int means a whole number (no decimal point)
No quotes around numbers when you want numeric values
lessons.starter:
students = 25
print(students)
print(type(students))

tasks.prompt: Create year_level = 9 and print Year level: and the value.

lessons.title: 2C. Decimal numbers: float
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: numbers with decimals
lessons.concept: Floats (float) are decimal numbers with a decimal point, like 19.95 or 1.6. Python uses them for decimal values.
learning: float means a decimal number (with a decimal point)
19.95 is a float (decimal), 19 is an int (whole number)
lessons.starter:
price = 19.95
print(price)
print(type(price))

tasks.prompt: Create height = 1.62 and print Height: and the value.

lessons.title: 2D. Text values: str
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: store and print text
lessons.concept: Strings (str) store text (words and sentences). When you assign text to a variable, keep it in quotes.
lessons.starter:
first_name = "Aroha"
print(first_name)
print(type(first_name))

tasks.prompt: Create city = "Auckland" (or your city) and print City: and the value.

lessons.title: 2E. True/False: bool
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: yes/no values
lessons.concept: Booleans (bool) have only two values: True and False (capital T/F). They represent yes/no or on/off.
learning: bool values are True or False (a yes/no type)
Python is case-sensitive: true is not the same as True
lessons.starter:
is_online = True
print(is_online)
print(type(is_online))

tasks.prompt: Create has_homework = False and print Homework done: and the value.

lessons.title: 2F. Good variable names
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: readable names
lessons.concept: Use clear names. For multiple words use snake_case (e.g. first_name). Python is case-sensitive: age, Age, and AGE are different variables.
lessons.starter:
first_name = "Sam"
last_name = "Lee"
print(first_name, last_name)

tasks.prompt: Create favourite_food using snake_case and print it.

lessons.title: Section 2 Test: Variables and types
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: int, float, str, bool
lessons.concept: Create a small profile using the right data types. This tests your understanding of variables, ints, floats, strings, and booleans.
learning: Use int (whole number) for values with no decimal point
Use float (decimal number) for values with a decimal point
Use str (text) for words and sentences, and bool (True/False) for yes/no values
lessons.starter:
# Section 2 Test: create a student profile
# Use variables: student_name (str), age (int), height_m (float), is_enrolled (bool)

tasks.prompt: Create student_name (str), age (int), height_m (float), is_enrolled (bool) and print each with a label.
tasks.hint:
Example: student_name = "Alex"
age = 14
height_m = 1.58
is_enrolled = True

lessons.title: 3A. Read input with input()
lessons.subtitle: Learn one small thing at a time: user interaction
lessons.concept: input() shows a prompt and waits for the user to type. It returns what the user typed as a string (text).
learning: input("Question: ") returns the user's text (a string)
The result is always a string (text)
Store it in a variable to use later
lessons.starter:
name = input("What is your name? ")
print(name)

tasks.prompt: Ask for the user's favourite subject and print it.

lessons.title: 3B. Combine text with +
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: build messages
lessons.concept: You can join strings (text) with +. This is called concatenation. Remember to include spaces inside quotes when needed.
learning: All parts must be strings (text) when using + this way
lessons.starter:
name = input("Name: ")
print("Hello " + name)

tasks.prompt: Ask for a city and print: Sam is from Auckland (using the inputs).
tasks.hint:
city = input("City: ")
print(name + " is from " + city)

lessons.title: Section 3 Test: Interactive greeting
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: input and string joining
lessons.concept: Build a small interactive program that asks questions and prints a personalised message.
learning: Use input() to get user data
lessons.starter:
# Section 3 Test
# Ask for name and favourite food, then print a sentence using both

tasks.prompt: Ask for name and favourite food, then print: <name> likes <food>.
tasks.hint:
name = input("Name: ")
food = input("Favourite food: ")
print(name + " likes " + food + ".")

lessons.title: 4A. Strings vs numbers
lessons.subtitle: Learn one small thing at a time: types affect behavior
lessons.concept: input() returns a string (text), so "10" + "20" becomes "1020" (text joined), not 30. To do maths, convert to numbers with int() (whole number) or float() (decimal number).
learning: int("10") converts text to an int (whole number)
lessons.starter:
first = input("First number: ")
second = input("Second number: ")
print(first + second)  # joins strings
print(int(first) + int(second))  # adds numbers

tasks.prompt: Run with 10 and 20, then explain in a comment what each print does.
tasks.hint: # first print joins text, second adds numbers

lessons.title: 4B. Convert to numbers
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: numeric conversion
lessons.concept: Use int() for whole numbers and float() for decimals. Converting input lets you calculate correctly.
learning: float() -> decimal number (with a decimal point)
Choose based on the data you expect
lessons.starter:
age_text = input("Age: ")
age = int(age_text)
print(age + 1)

tasks.prompt: Ask for a price as input, convert to float, add 2.5, and print Total: with the result.

lessons.subsection: 4C. str() and combining text with numbers
lessons.title: 4C. Convert numbers to text for messages
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: build output safely
lessons.concept: When joining with +, all parts must be strings (text). Use str() to convert a number to text in a message.
learning: str(30) turns a number into text (a string)
print can also separate values with commas
lessons.starter:
result = 10 + 20
print("Result: " + str(result))

tasks.prompt: Calculate 7 * 6, store it in answer, and print Answer: 42 using str().

lessons.title: Section 4 Test: Mini calculator
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: input, conversion, output
lessons.concept: Create a small calculator that reads two numbers, converts them, calculates, and prints clear results.
learning: Use str() to convert numbers to text, or commas when printing
lessons.starter: # Section 4 Test: add two numbers entered by the user and print Sum: <value>

tasks.prompt: Ask for two numbers (use float), add them, and print Sum: with the total.
tasks.hint:
a = float(input("First: "))
b = float(input("Second: "))
print("Sum: " + str(a + b))

lessons.title: 5A. Change letter case
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: transform text
lessons.focus: upper(), lower(), methods return new strings
lessons.concept: Strings have methods (functions attached to the string). .upper() and .lower() return a new string; they do not change the original.
lessons.starter:
course = "Python for Beginners"
print(course.upper())
print(course.lower())
print(course)

tasks.prompt: Create word = "kia ora" and print it in uppercase.

lessons.title: 5B. Search and replace text
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: locate and change parts
lessons.concept: .find() returns the index of text (or -1 if not found). .replace() returns a new string with replacements made.
lessons.starter:
course = "Python for Beginners"
print(course.find("for"))
print(course.replace("Beginners", "Absolute Beginners"))

tasks.prompt: Replace "Python" with "Coding" in course and print the result.

lessons.title: 5C. Access characters and check membership
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: positions and searching
lessons.concept: You can access a character by index: course[0] is the first character. The in operator checks whether text appears in a string and returns True/False.
learning: "Python" in course returns True/False (a bool value)
lessons.starter:
course = "Python for Beginners"
print(course[0])
print("Python" in course)
print("Java" in course)

tasks.prompt: Print the first character of your own name variable and check if 'a' is in it.

lessons.title: Section 5 Test: String skills
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: methods, indexing, in
lessons.concept: Use multiple string skills on one piece of text to show you understand how strings work.
learning: Use at least one string (text) method
lessons.starter:
text = "python programming"
# Section 5 Test: work with the text variable

tasks.prompt: Print text in uppercase, print text[0], and print whether "gram" is in text.

lessons.title: 6A. Add, subtract, multiply, divide
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: core maths operators
lessons.concept: Python can calculate using arithmetic operators: + addition, - subtraction, * multiplication, / division (returns a float).
lessons.starter:
print(10 + 3)
print(10 - 3)
print(10 * 3)
print(10 / 3)

tasks.prompt: Print the result of 7 * 6 and 20 - 8.

lessons.title: 6B. Whole division, remainder, powers
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: more operators
lessons.concept: // gives whole-number division, % gives the remainder, and ** raises to a power.
lessons.starter:
print(10 // 3)
print(10 % 3)
print(2 ** 3)

tasks.prompt: Print 23 // 5 and 23 % 5.

lessons.title: 6C. Order of operations and shortcuts
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: control calculations
lessons.concept: Multiplication/division happen before addition/subtraction unless parentheses change the order. Augmented assignment like x += 3 is shorthand for x = x + 3.
lessons.starter:
print(10 + 3 * 2)
print((10 + 3) * 2)
x = 10
x += 5
print(x)

tasks.prompt: Create score = 20, subtract 7 using -=, and print Score: and the value.

lessons.title: Section 6 Test: Number challenge
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: arithmetic in context
lessons.concept: Solve a small real-world number problem using arithmetic operators and variables.
lessons.starter:
# Section 6 Test: 23 lollies shared between 4 friends
lollies = 23
friends = 4

tasks.prompt: Using lollies and friends, print how many each friend gets (whole number) and how many are left over.
tasks.hint:
print("Each:", lollies // friends)
print("Left over:", lollies % friends)

lessons.title: 7A. Compare values (True/False)
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: comparisons
lessons.concept: Comparison operators compare values and produce booleans: True or False. Use == to check equality (not =, which assigns).
lessons.starter:
x = 3
print(x > 2)
print(x == 3)
print(x != 3)

tasks.prompt: Set age = 14 and print whether age >= 13 and whether age < 18.

lessons.title: 7B. Combine conditions with and/or/not
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: boolean logic
lessons.concept: Logical operators combine conditions: and needs both True, or needs at least one True, not flips True/False.
lessons.starter:
price = 25
print(price > 10 and price < 30)
print(price > 10 or price > 100)
print(not price > 100)

tasks.prompt: Create temperature = 18 and print whether it is between 15 and 25 (inclusive of 15 and 25).

lessons.title: 7C. Make choices in code
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: branching
lessons.concept: if runs a block when a condition is True. elif checks another condition if previous ones were False. else runs if none matched. Indentation defines the block.
learning: Python checks conditions top to bottom

tasks.prompt: Change temperature so the output includes Cold day, or add your own elif branch.
tasks.hint: Try temperature = 5 or add elif temperature > 10:

lessons.title: Section 7 Test: Decision maker
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: comparisons, logic, if/elif/else
lessons.concept: Write a program that makes decisions based on a value using if/elif/else.
lessons.starter:
# Section 7 Test: set score and print a grade
score = 75

tasks.prompt: If score >= 80 print Merit, elif score >= 50 print Achieved, else print Not yet.

lessons.title: 8A. Repeat while a condition is true
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: counting
lessons.concept: A while loop repeats a block as long as its condition is True. Use it when you want to repeat based on a condition.
learning: Indented code is the loop body
Loop stops when condition becomes False
lessons.starter:
i = 1
while i <= 5:
    print(i)
    i = i + 1

tasks.prompt: Change the loop to print numbers 1 to 3.

lessons.title: 8B. Avoid infinite loops
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: counters and updates
lessons.focus: loop variable update, infinite loop prevention
lessons.concept: You must change something inside the loop (like i += 1 or count -= 1) so the condition can become False. Otherwise the loop may run forever.
learning: Forgetting updates can cause infinite loops
Test loops with small ranges first
lessons.starter:
count = 3
while count > 0:
    print("Count:", count)
    count -= 1
print("Go!")

tasks.prompt: Make it count down from 5 to 1 and then print Go!.

lessons.title: Section 8 Test: Loop challenge
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: while loops
lessons.concept: Use a while loop to produce repeated output correctly.
lessons.starter: # Section 8 Test: print numbers 1 to 5 using a while loop

tasks.prompt: Use a while loop to print numbers 1 to 5, one per line.

lessons.title: 9A. Store multiple items in a list
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: ordered collections
lessons.concept: Lists store multiple items in order using square brackets. Indexing starts at 0. Negative indexes count from the end (-1 is last).
lessons.starter:
names = ["John", "Bob", "Mosh", "Sam"]
print(names)
print(names[0])
print(names[-1])

tasks.prompt: Create a list of 3 fruits and print the first and last fruit.

lessons.title: 9B. Update and inspect lists
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: append, insert, len, in
lessons.focus: append, insert, remove, len, in, mutability
lessons.concept: Lists are mutable (changeable). You can append/insert/remove items. len() gives the number of items and in checks if an item exists.
learning: len(list) counts items, item in list checks membership
lessons.starter:
numbers = [1, 2, 3]
numbers.append(4)
print(numbers)
print(len(numbers))
print(2 in numbers)

tasks.prompt: Start with nums = [5, 10], append 15, and print Length: with len(nums).

lessons.title: 9C. Iterate over items and numbers
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: for loops
lessons.concept: for loops iterate over sequences like lists. range() generates numbers: range(5) gives 0-4, range(5,10) gives 5-9, range(5,10,2) steps by 2.
learning: for item in list: visits each item
for i in range(5): repeats with 0-4

tasks.prompt: Use range(2, 11, 2) to print even numbers 2 to 10.

lessons.title: Section 9 Test: Lists and loops
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: collections and iteration
lessons.concept: Use a list and a loop together to process multiple values.
lessons.starter:
names = ["Aroha", "Ben", "Mia"]
# Section 9 Test

tasks.prompt: Use a for loop to print Hello, <name> for each name in the list.
tasks.hint:
for name in names:
    print("Hello, " + name)

lessons.section: Section 10: Tuples and Putting It All Together
lessons.title: 10A. Fixed collections with tuples
lessons.subtitle: Tiny exercise: tuple basics
lessons.concept: Tuples are like lists but immutable (cannot be changed after creation). They use parentheses and support methods like count() and index().
learning: count() and index() work on tuples
lessons.starter:
numbers = (1, 2, 3, 3)
print(numbers)
print(numbers.count(3))
print(numbers.index(2))

tasks.prompt: Create a tuple of three colours and print the tuple and the index of one colour.

lessons.section: Section 10: Tuples and Putting It All Together
lessons.title: Final Section Test: Mini program
lessons.subtitle: Put it together: core Python basics
lessons.focus: variables, input/conversion or strings, decisions, loops/lists
lessons.concept: Create a small program that combines multiple concepts from the course (variables, strings/numbers, conditionals, and/or loops/lists).
lessons.starter:
# Final Test (example starter): number list total
numbers = [2, 4, 6]
total = 0
# add code to calculate total and print it

tasks.prompt: Use a for loop to add the numbers in the list and print Total: 12.
